one_liner: Archived Go BLAKE2b with AVX2/AVX/SSSE3 assembly, about 4x its pure-Go fallback and faster than 2016-era Go SHA-256/SHA-512.
what_it_does: A Go package (package name blake2b) that computes BLAKE2b digests and prefix MACs through the standard hash.Hash interface. Its API is the same as dchest/blake2b: New(*Config), New512(), New256(), NewMAC(size, key), Sum512 and Sum256. Config also exposes the salt, personalization and tree-hashing parameters (fanout, depth, leaf size, node offset). It is a drop-in swap for dchest/blake2b but not for golang.org/x/crypto/blake2b, whose constructors take a key and return an error.
how_it_is_fast: The BLAKE2b compression function is hand-written in Go assembly. The AVX2 path follows Samuel Neves' blake2-avx2 code: one YMM register holds a whole 4x64-bit row, so each G step works on four columns at once, and VPERMQ does the diagonalize/undiagonalize. The AVX and SSE paths follow the reference BLAKE2 sse/blake2b.c and use two XMM registers per row. The 32/24/16-bit rotations are done with PSHUFB/VPSHUFB byte shuffles, and the 63-bit rotation with add+shift+xor. The loop over 128-byte blocks runs inside the assembly, and the CPU check (CPUID/XGETBV) runs once at package init to pick AVX2, then AVX, then SSSE3, then generic Go.
when_to_use: Legacy Go code that already imports it or dchest/blake2b, on amd64, where you want roughly 1.7x (64 B) to 3.9x (128 KiB) more BLAKE2b throughput with no API change.
Bulk checksums or bit-rot checks of large buffers (8 KiB and up) on AVX2 x86-64, where the SIMD path is 3-4x the pure-Go path in the README tables.
You need BLAKE2b's salt, personalization or tree-hashing parameters (as in bt2sum's tree mode). golang.org/x/crypto/blake2b only takes a size and a key.
Reading or benchmarking a small, self-contained reference for how BLAKE2b maps onto AVX2/SSSE3 in Go assembly.
when_not_to_use: New code: the repo is archived, and the Minio maintainers said in 2018 (issues #29-#31) that they had switched to golang.org/x/crypto/blake2b. That package has its own AVX2/AVX/SSE4 assembly and adds BLAKE2Xb and state (un)marshalling.

Non-amd64 targets such as arm64, Apple M1 or Graviton only get the generic Go code (the NEON request, issue #15, is still open). A 2021 HN user saw Go's hardware-accelerated SHA-1/SHA-256 reach about 2.5 GB/s on an M1, far above this package there.

Machines without SSSE3 or AVX, such as the SSE2-only Celeron in issue #24, where it ran at the same speed as the cgo codahale/blake2. On an Atom C2750 (issue #11) the SSE path reached only 59 MB/s at 128 KiB.
Small messages: the gain drops to 1.7-1.9x at 64-128 B, where per-call setup and finalization dominate.

You need encoding.BinaryMarshaler state snapshots, BLAKE2Xb/XOF output, BLAKE2s, or a tagged, module-aware release. None exist here; pkg.go.dev shows only the pseudo-version v0.0.0-...-3f5f724 from 2016-07-23.

integration.form: module (go get github.com/minio/blake2b-simd; no go.mod and no tagged releases, so it resolves to a 2016 pseudo-version) or source-drop (about 20 files)
integration.min_toolchain: Go gc toolchain. CI tested only Go 1.5/1.6 on Travis and AppVeyor, and support for modern Go is not documented. It uses old-style '// +build' constraints. The .s files are pre-assembled into BYTE sequences, so building does not need asm2plan9s; that tool is only for editing the assembly.
integration.platforms: amd64 with runtime dispatch (AVX2 > AVX > SSSE3 > pure Go). Every other architecture gets the pure-Go path.
integration.thread_safety: not documented. hash.Hash values returned by New/New512/NewMAC hold mutable state (use one per goroutine). Sum512/Sum256 build a local digest on each call.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same API as dchest/blake2b, from which the pure-Go baseline comes, so swapping the import is enough. Against stdlib crypto/sha256 or crypto/sha512 it is only hash.Hash-compatible and gives different digests.

gotchas: The package name is blake2b but the import path ends in blake2b-simd, and it clashes with golang.org/x/crypto/blake2b. Importing both needs an alias, and the two have different constructor signatures: New512() here versus New512(key) (hash.Hash, error) in x/crypto.
New(c) writes Size=64 back into the caller's Config when c.Size is 0, and NewMAC panics instead of returning an error for invalid sizes or keys.

compress_amd64.go has no build constraint, while compress_noasm.go also defines compress under the 'noasm'/'appengine' tags. The documented '-tags noasm' escape hatch therefore looks like it would fail to compile on amd64, as would gccgo (cpuid.go is '!gccgo'). Not tested here.

The README benchmark names (BenchmarkHash*) no longer match benchmarks_test.go (BenchmarkSize*), and nothing in the repo benchmarks it against x/crypto/blake2b. Issue #32 (2018) asking for that comparison is still open.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: It is the only Go entry. blake2b_simd (oconnor663) is the Rust BLAKE2b to use outside Go, and BLAKE3 is much faster if you can change algorithms. Pick this over minio's own sha256-simd only when you need BLAKE2b digests on amd64 rather than SHA-256 compatibility or ARM64 acceleration.
verified_claims_summary: These are first-party 2016 go test benchmarks with an unstated Go version (CI used Go 1.5/1.6). On a Xeon E5-2620 v3 the AVX2 path hashes 128 KiB at 918.93 MB/s versus 233.37 MB/s for the package's own pure-Go path (3.94x). AVX is 3.28x and SSE 2.85x on a 2.7 GHz MacBook Pro i7, with gains of only 1.7-1.9x at 64-128 B. A 1 MiB stdlib comparison on the Xeon gives 850.64 MB/s versus Go SHA-256 at 189.58, SHA-512 at 306.33 and MD5 at 607.48 MB/s, all before Go had SHA-NI or ARMv8 SHA acceleration.
status_note: Archived. The last code commit was 2016-07-23, and Minio itself moved to golang.org/x/crypto/blake2b in 2018. It is Apache-2.0, tiny and dependency-free, and pkg.go.dev still lists 314 known importers, so it is safe to vendor but should not be chosen for new work.
